Edinburgh is not a very big city, but it is beautiful. The buildings in the centre are very old. People from many countries are here. They are from America, from Germany, from China and from Italy. We hear many languages in the centre.
The weather is awful! It is cold and wet today. “Where is the sun?” Zilola says. “It is not in Scotland!” I say. “It is on holiday, too.”

Our hotel is near the centre. It is in an old building. The people in the hotel are lovely. “Good morning! How are you today?” they say. “We are fine, thank you. But the weather is awful.” “Yes, but this is Scotland!”

Now we are in a café. Zilola's tea is really good, and my coffee is OK. “Look at this map,” Zilola says. “Where is the old school of doctors?” “It is here, near the hospital.” Zilola is a doctor, and it is interesting for her.

text: From Monday to Friday I am very busy. I get up early, I go to university, and in the evening I work in a café. But at the weekend my life is not the same!

On Sunday I visit my mum and dad. They live in a small village near the town. I leave home at ten o'clock and go by bus. Mum always makes a fantastic lunch. After lunch Dad and I walk in the garden, and he speaks about his work. He paints, and his studio is in the house.

text: My little brother Bobur is five years old, and he has one favourite word: “Why?” He asks questions all day.

Navoi was never married, and there were no children in his house. But there were always students, writers, musicians and scientists. He died in 1501, when he was sixty years old. Today there are streets, theatres and a city with his name. People still read his books and love them.

text: I was sixteen when I had my first date. Her name was Nilufar, and she was in my class. I liked her for a long time, but I didn't speak to her. Then one day I asked, “Do you want to go to the cinema on Saturday?” She said, “Yes, OK.” I was the most lucky boy in the school!
On Saturday I got up early. I cleaned my shoes and washed my hair two times. I wanted to look special.
We met in the square at five o'clock. I arrived at four! Nilufar arrived at ten past five. She looked wonderful. “Sorry I'm late,” she said.

First we went to a coffee bar. I ordered two orange juices. I was really nervous, and my orange juice went all over the table! Nilufar laughed. “It's OK,” she said. Then we talked about school, music and films. She was interested in everything.
After that we walked to the cinema. The film started at six. It was a film about a tourist in India. It wasn't very good, but we enjoyed it. We ate ice-cream and laughed a lot.

After the film I walked home with her. It was a warm evening, and the sun went down behind the houses. “Thank you. I had a really good time,” she said. That was twelve years ago. Last year Nilufar and I got married. And we still go to the cinema every Saturday!

text: Last January my friends and I went on a winter holiday. We went to the mountains near Tashkent for four days. We stayed in a small hotel with a view of the mountains.
We arrived on Thursday evening. It was dark and very cold, and there was a lot of snow. We had dinner in the hotel: hot soup, pasta and tea. Then we played cards and went to bed early.

On Friday the sun was bright, and we went skiing. It was my first time. I didn't ski well. I sat in the snow more than I skied! My friend Jasur was really good, and he showed me what to do. In the afternoon I skied ten metres without falling. I was very happy.

On Saturday we didn't ski. We went ice-skating on a lake in the morning. In the afternoon we walked in the forest and took a lot of photographs. In the evening there was a party in the hotel. We listened to music and danced with other tourists. Some of them were from India, and they showed us an Indian dance.
On Sunday morning I wanted to ski again. This time I didn't fall! Then we had a big lunch, and at three o'clock we left.
It wasn't a cheap holiday, and I was tired after it. But the mountains, the snow and the sun were really special. Next winter I want to go for a week.

text: Last Saturday our class went to the history museum in the city centre. Our teacher, Mrs Yusupova, organised the tour. We met in the square in front of the museum at ten o'clock.
I didn't want to go. “Museums are for old people,” I said to my friend Akmal. But I was wrong!

The museum was free for students. A guide showed us around. She was young and funny, and she didn't speak like a book. First she showed us very old things: cups, plates and knives. People made them three thousand years ago. “Did they have phones?” Akmal asked. Everybody laughed.

Then we saw clothes, books and maps from different times. I really liked a map of the Silk Road. Tourists and traders travelled on it with horses and camels. They carried silk, tea and paper from China to Europe.
On the second floor there was a special room for children. We played old games there. I played a game with small stones, and I didn't win once! We listened to old music, too, and two girls danced.

We finished at one o'clock. After the tour we had lunch in a coffee bar next to the museum. I had a sandwich and orange juice. “Did you enjoy it?” Mrs Yusupova asked. “Yes, I did,” I said. “I was really interested. Can we come again?” She smiled. “You didn't want to come!” “That was me three hours ago,” I said.

text: Everybody in my family can do something well.

My grandfather is a farmer. He is seventy, but he can still work all day. He can drive a tractor and ride a horse really well. He can't use a computer, and he is a little bit afraid of the Net. “I can't understand it,” he says. “A horse is safe. The Internet is dangerous!”

My sister Madina is an interpreter. She can speak four languages fluently: Uzbek, Russian, English and Arabic. She works at the airport and helps tourists with problems. Yesterday a young man came to her. “What's the matter?” she asked. His passport was lost. Madina helped him and he didn't miss his plane. Madina can also play the guitar, but she can't draw.

My brother Sanjar is a student. He wants to be a pilot and fly big planes worldwide. He is tall and he is a good athlete: he can swim fast and run for an hour. He can play chess, too, but he can't play a musical instrument.

And me? I am twelve. I can't drive and I can't fly a plane. But I can use a computer very well. I can send messages, chat with my friends and find the news on the Net. I also teach my grandfather. Now he can send a message to my uncle in America – very slowly! “Try again, Grandpa,” I say. “It is easy!” We share everything in our family. They help me, and I can help them.

text: It is nine o'clock in the morning at Tashkent airport. Mr Brown is a tourist from England. He can't speak Uzbek or Russian, and he has a problem.
He goes to the ticket machine. He wants a ticket for the train to the city centre. He pushes the green button. Nothing happens. He pushes it again. Nothing! “Oh no,” he says.

A young woman stops. “Excuse me, what's the matter? Can I help you?” “Oh, yes, please! Can you speak English?” “A little bit.” “I can't use this machine. I can't understand it.” “No problem. First you push the blue button. Now you can choose English. Then you push the green button.” “It works! Thank you!”
“Can you tell me the time, please?” “Yes, it's ten past nine.” “Oh, my train! Is it far?” “No. Can you see that door? Go there and turn left.”

Mr Brown runs. But then he stops. Where is his passport? It isn't in his bag. It isn't in his coat. He is afraid. He can't go anywhere without it! “Sir! Sir!” It is the young woman. “Your passport! It was next to the ticket machine.” “Oh, thank you very much! You are very kind. Can I offer you a coffee?” “I'm sorry, I can't. I have a lesson at ten. I am a student, and I want to be an interpreter.”
“You can do it,” says Mr Brown. “You speak English really well!”

text: Sabina Rahimova is only fourteen, but she is a famous athlete in her town. She is a swimmer. She can swim a hundred metres in one minute!
Sabina started when she was five. “I was afraid of water,” she says. “I couldn't swim, and I didn't want to try. But my mum said, ‘You can do it. Try!’ Now I can't live without water.”

Her day is not easy. She gets up at five o'clock and swims for two hours before school. After school she swims again. She can't go out with friends in the evening, because she goes to bed at nine. She can't eat a lot of cake or chocolate. “Sometimes it is boring,” she says. “But I want to be the best.”

She can do other things, too. She can ride a bike and a horse. She can play chess really well – she plays with her grandfather every Sunday, and he can't win! She can speak English a little bit, because she goes to other countries. But she can't draw. “My horses look like dogs!” she says.
Is swimming dangerous? “No, it's safe. But it is hard. Last year I hurt my arm, and I couldn't swim for two months. I really missed it.”
Sabina has a blog, and young swimmers send her messages from all the world. What does she tell them? “Don't be afraid. Start slowly, try again and again, and one day you can fly!”

text: My grandmother is seventy-five, and she says, “The Net is a dangerous thing!” My little brother is ten, and he says, “I can't live without it!” Who is right?

What can you do on the Net? Nearly everything! You can send messages to friends and chat with people worldwide. You can read the news, listen to the radio and watch films. You can buy plane tickets and find a hotel. You can learn history, geography and science. You can learn a language, too: my sister learned English with videos, and now she speaks fluently.

People can share things. A farmer in a small village can sell his fruit to people in the city. A doctor can help a person in another country. A young musician can play the guitar for a million people.

But there are problems. Some people can't stop. My brother plays computer games for hours. He doesn't go out, and he doesn't do his homework. Some things on the Net are not true, and children can't always understand that. And it is not always safe: bad people can use the Net, too.
So what is the answer? I think the Net is like a car. A car is a good thing, but you learn to drive it, and you drive carefully. We can use the Net, but it can't be our life.
My grandmother has a mobile phone now. She can send me messages – very slowly! “It is not so dangerous,” she says.

text: Captain Aziz Karimov is a pilot. He is forty-five, and he flies a jumbo jet. His plane can carry four hundred people, and it can fly from Tashkent to New York in twelve hours.

“People think a pilot's job is dangerous,” he says. “It isn't. Flying is very safe – a plane is safer than a car. But it isn't easy. You can't make mistakes.” What can a good pilot do? He can use hundreds of buttons, of course. He can understand the weather. He can speak English fluently, because pilots worldwide communicate in English. And he can stay quiet when there is a problem. “A pilot can't be afraid,” Aziz says. “Four hundred people are behind you.”

Aziz can fly a jumbo jet, but there are a lot of things he can't do! “I can't ride a horse,” he says. “I tried once, and I hurt my arm. I can't play a musical instrument. I can't draw. And I can't use the ticket machine at the station! My daughter always helps me.”
He can't be at home a lot, and that is the hard part of his job. He often misses birthdays. But he can chat with his family on the Net and send them messages from anywhere.
When he is at home, he doesn't fly. He works in his garden, slowly and quietly. “In my job everything is fast,” he says. “At home I can be slow. I need that.”

text: Last Friday I wanted to send a message to my friend Kamola. “Can you come to my house at six? We can watch a film and eat cake,” I wrote. I pushed the button. Send!
Six o'clock: no Kamola. Seven o'clock: no Kamola, and no answer. I was a little bit angry. “She can't be so busy,” I thought.

At half past seven the phone rang. It was not Kamola. It was Mr Salimov, my history teacher! “Good evening, Dilnoza,” he said. “Thank you for your kind message. But I'm afraid I can't come. I can't eat cake – I am on a diet. And I have forty tests to read.”
Oh no! Kamola Salimova and Mr Salimov are next to each other in my phone. I sent the message to my teacher!
“I'm so sorry, Mr Salimov,” I said. “It was a mistake.” He laughed. “No problem. It happens. But can I ask you something? Can you send me your homework, too? I can't find it.”
My homework! I didn't do it. “Yes, of course,” I said slowly. “Tomorrow.”
Then I sent the message again – to the right person. Kamola arrived at eight with a big smile. “What's the matter? You look red!” I told her the story, and she laughed for ten minutes.
So we didn't watch a film. We ate the cake, and then Kamola helped me with my history homework. Now I always read the name before I push “Send”.

text: My grandfather is eighty years old. He was a farmer all his life, and he lives in a small village. He didn't go to university. But he is the cleverest person I know. He can do nearly everything!

He can ride a horse really well. When he was young, he could ride for six hours without stopping. He can drive a tractor, too, and he can repair it when there is a problem. He never calls a mechanic. He can make things. He made the tables and the doors in his house. He can play the dutar – it is an Uzbek musical instrument – and he can sing old songs. He can play chess, and nobody in the village can win against him.
He can tell you about the weather tomorrow. He looks at the sky and says, “Rain in the afternoon.” He is always right. He can't explain it. “I just know,” he says.
There are some things he can't do. He can't swim, because there was no river in his village. He can't use a computer, and he can't speak English. “I am too old for the Net,” he says.

But last summer I showed him my blog, with photographs of his horse and his garden. People worldwide wrote kind messages. He was very interested. “Can you teach me?” he asked. Now he can turn on the computer and read the news. He does it slowly, but he tries every day. He is a little bit famous now!

text: It is Saturday afternoon. Kamila and her friend Nigora are in the town centre. They went to a bookshop in the morning, and now they feel hungry and thirsty. “I'd like a snack,” says Nigora. “Just a snack? I'd like a real lunch!” says Kamila. So they go to the Garden Restaurant. It has tables in a beautiful garden.
They sit down and wait. The waiter comes immediately with the menu and a smile. He is very polite.
“Good afternoon. What would you like to drink?”
“I'd like a bottle of mineral water, please,” says Kamila.
“Still or sparkling?”
“Sparkling, please.”
“And I'd like some apple juice,” says Nigora.
Then they look at the menu. There are a lot of dishes: soup, chicken, fish, meat and vegetables.
“Are you ready to order?” asks the waiter.
“Yes. I'd like the tomato soup and then the salmon with rice,” says Kamila.
“I'm sorry, we don't have any salmon today. Would you like the chicken? It is very good.”

The food comes on big plates and it is delicious. For dessert Kamila has a slice of chocolate cake. Nigora has apple pie and tea with a little sugar. They nearly forget the time!
“Can we have the bill, please?” asks Kamila. The meal is not expensive, and the service is excellent. “Maybe we can come again next Saturday,” says Nigora. “Good idea!”

text: It is Sunday morning in the Karimov family. On Sundays Dad makes breakfast for everybody, and he likes to play the waiter.
“Good morning, ladies and gentlemen!” he says with a smile. “What would you like for breakfast?”

“I'd like some cereal with milk, please,” says Lola. She is seven. “And some chocolate cake.” “I'm sorry, we don't have any chocolate cake. Would you like some bread and jam?” “Yes, please! A lot of jam.”

“And for you, sir?” “I'd like two eggs, some bread and a glass of apple juice,” says Bobur. He is fifteen, and he is always hungry. “Anything else?” “Yes. Some cheese and a tomato, please. And maybe a banana.” “That is not a breakfast. That is a lunch!”
“And for the lady?” Mum smiles. “Just a cup of tea with a little sugar, please. And a slice of bread.” “Would you like some jam?” “No, thank you. Just bread.”

text: Madina is a student, and she wants to be a doctor. Today she has a lesson about food. “What is a healthy diet?” the teacher asks.

“First, you need a lot of fruit and vegetables,” the teacher says. “Tomatoes, onions, beans, apples – they are all good for you. Eat some every day. Second, you need fish, chicken or meat, but not a lot. Fish is the best. Third, you need bread, rice or cereal. They give you energy.”
“What about sugar?” asks Madina. “Just a little. Cakes, jam and chocolate are nice, but they are not good for your teeth. And don't forget water! Drink mineral water, not Coke.”

After the lesson Madina thinks about her diet. What does she usually eat? For breakfast she has coffee with a lot of sugar. For lunch she has a hamburger or a slice of pizza, because she is always in a hurry. In the afternoon she has a snack: chocolate cake! For dinner she has pasta with mayonnaise.
“Oh dear,” she thinks. “There aren't any vegetables in my diet. There isn't any fruit. I'd like to be a doctor, and I eat like this?”
So she makes a plan. Tomorrow she would like cereal and an apple for breakfast, chicken soup and a mixed salad for lunch, and fish with rice for dinner.
“And chocolate cake?” her friend asks. Madina smiles. “Maybe a small slice. On Sundays!”

text: It is Friday evening. Sardor and his wife Malika are at a new restaurant in the city centre. Today is Malika's birthday.
“Good evening. A table for two?” asks the waiter. “Yes, please. Could we have a table near the window?” “Of course. Follow me, please.”
They sit down, and the waiter brings the menu. “Would you like something to drink?” “I'd like some orange juice, please,” says Malika. “And a bottle of sparkling mineral water for me,” says Sardor.

There are a lot of dishes on the menu. “What would you like?” Sardor asks. “I'm not very hungry. Maybe just a mixed salad and some fish.” “I'm really hungry! I'd like the onion soup, and then the chicken with rice and vegetables.”
The waiter writes the order. “Would you like any side orders? Bread? Beans?” “Some bread, please.”
The food is very good. Malika's salmon is fresh, and Sardor's chicken is hot and delicious. They talk and smile, and they nearly forget the time.

text: Every morning Mrs Azimova makes three lunch boxes for her children. It is not easy, because the three children would like three different lunches!

Jasur is sixteen. He plays football and runs marathons, so he is always hungry. He would like a big lunch: two chicken sandwiches, some rice, a tomato, an apple and a bottle of juice. “And maybe a slice of cake?” he asks. “There isn't any cake,” his mother says. “There are some bananas.”

Kamila is thirteen. She doesn't eat meat. She would like a mixed salad with beans, some bread and cheese, and some fruit. She doesn't like onions, so her mother never puts any onion in the salad. She drinks just mineral water.

Timur is eight. He would like only two things: bread with jam, and chocolate. “You can't have chocolate for lunch,” his mother says. “Would you like an egg sandwich?” “No!” “Some soup?” “No!” “A little rice with chicken?” “OK. But with mayonnaise.” At seven o'clock the three boxes are ready. But today there is a problem. In a hurry, Mrs Azimova swaps the boxes!
At lunch time Jasur opens his box and finds a salad with beans. Kamila finds rice with chicken and mayonnaise. And Timur? He finds two big chicken sandwiches, and he eats them all!
“How was lunch?” their mother asks in the evening. “I was hungry all day,” says Jasur. “I ate only the bread,” says Kamila. “It was the best lunch!” says Timur.

text: Farhod is a waiter in a coffee shop near the park. He meets a lot of customers every day. Some are polite, and some are not!

Yesterday morning an old woman came in. She smiled and said, “Good morning! Could I have a cup of tea and a slice of apple pie, please?” “Of course. Would you like some sugar?” “Just a little, please.” She waited for her order and read a book. When Farhod came with the plate, she said, “Thank you so much. The service here is always so good.” Farhod felt very pleased.
In the afternoon a young man came in. He didn't say hello. He didn't look at the menu. “Coffee. Now,” he said. “Would you like anything else?” “A sandwich. Chicken. Immediately!”

Farhod was polite, as usual. He brought the coffee and the sandwich in two minutes. The young man took the sandwich. “This is ham! I said chicken!” “It is chicken, sir.” The man looked again. It was chicken. He didn't say sorry.
Then he pulled the sugar bottle from the next table, and all the sugar went on the floor. The other customers looked at him. His face was red.
Farhod came with a smile. “No problem, sir. Would you like another coffee?” The young man was quiet for a moment. Then he said slowly, “Yes… please. And… sorry.”
“You see?” the old woman said to Farhod. “A smile is the best teacher.”

“What are you wearing? It's cold in Tashkent.” “I'm wearing a jumper and warm socks.” “And a scarf?” “Mum, I'm sitting in my room! Nobody wears a scarf at home.” “Do you have a cold? Your voice is strange.” “No, I don't have a cold. I have a little headache, because I'm working a lot.”
“What is your friend Nozima doing?” “She is sleeping. She finished her exams yesterday.” “And is the window open?” “No, Mum. It's closed.” “Good. Is the TV on?” “No. I turned it off an hour ago.”

text: My name is Shahzod. I am eighteen and I am in my last year at school. Next month I have my exams, so I am a little nervous. I study carefully every evening, because these exams are very important for my future.

After the exams I am going to have a holiday. My best friend Otabek and I have a great plan. We are going to travel across Europe by train! We are going to take only our rucksacks and a small tent. Our flight to Belgium is on 1 July. First we are going to visit the old towns, with their canals and bridges, and have a boat trip. Then we are going to go to England by train. The train goes along a long tunnel under the sea!

The trip is not going to cost a lot of money. We are going to use local transport, eat cheap food and sleep in the tent. Sometimes we are going to travel overnight on the train. I hope the weather is going to be good. I want sunshine, not rain! I am going to bring souvenirs for my family.

In September I am going to begin university. I am going to study modern languages and economics. My sister studied medicine and now she is a doctor, but I am not interested in biology. I'd like to be a journalist. I am going to move to Tashkent and live on the campus.

What am I going to do after university? I don't know yet. Maybe I am going to work abroad. Maybe I am going to ride a motorbike across Africa or go on safari in Zambia! My father says, “Grow up, Shahzod!” But I think plans are important, and dreams are important, too.

text: Our teacher asked us a question today: “What are you going to be when you grow up?” Everybody in my class has a plan!

Sardor is going to be a doctor. He is going to study medicine at university. “It is going to be hard,” he says. “Six years of biology and exams! But I want to work in developing countries and help people there.”

Nilufar is going to be a journalist. She is going to study modern languages, and then she is going to work abroad. “I want to travel all year round and write about important events,” she says. She is not nervous about it.
Jahongir is going to be a painter. “Not a house painter!” he explains quickly. “An artist.” His father wants him to study economics, but Jahongir is not interested in money.

Kamila is going to study physics. She hopes to work for a big research company. “I am going to build a tunnel under the sea, or a very long bridge,” she says. And me? I don't know yet. I like psychology, because people are interesting. But I also like boats and the sea. Maybe I am going to work on a cruise ship and listen to people's problems!
My mother is a housewife, and she has a good answer. “You don't need to know now,” she says. “Study carefully, try many things, and your future is going to find you.” I hope she is right.

Then we are going to take a train to Amsterdam. It is a city of canals and bridges. We are going to have a boat trip along the canals and ride bikes, because everybody rides a bike there.

After that we are going to travel east to Germany, and then south to Italy. We aren't going to fly. We are going to travel by train, because we can see the mountains, the villages and the lakes from the window. One train goes overnight, so we are going to sleep on it and save money.
We aren't going to stay in expensive hotels. We are going to stay in hostels and carry everything in our rucksacks. We are going to eat in small local bistros, not in restaurants.

“I am going to fail,” he says to his sister, Lola. “I don't know anything!”

“First, you are going to close your books. Second, you are going to eat a banana and drink some warm milk. Then you are going to sleep. Tomorrow you are going to get up early, have a good breakfast and walk to school slowly. You aren't going to speak to nervous friends before the exam.”

“And in the exam?” “Read every question carefully. Begin with the easy questions. Don't hurry, but don't lose time. If you don't understand a question, read it again. And remember: one exam is not all your future.”
Aziz closes his books. “How do you know all this?” “It is my job to know! And I failed my first exam, because I studied all night.”

“Is it dangerous?” my mother asked. She was nervous. “Not if you are careful. We are going to drive slowly, and we are not going to walk at night.”

“What are your plans for the summer?” he asks.
“I am going to work in my uncle's bistro,” says Jasur. “I want to practise my English with tourists.”

text: It is 31 December, and I am writing my plans for next year. I do this every year. Last year I had ten plans, and I did only two! This year I am going to be careful. I am going to have only five.

First, I am going to learn English well. I am going to read one English book every month and learn ten new words every day. In the summer I am going to take an exam. I hope I am going to pass! Second, I am going to do more sport. I am going to ride my bike to school, not go by bus. And I am going to swim two times a week. My friend Sardor is going to come with me, so I can't be lazy.
Third, I am going to help my mother more. She is a housewife, and she works all day. I am going to wash the dishes every evening and clean my room on Saturdays.
Fourth, I am going to save money. I am not going to buy chocolate every day. I want a motorbike when I am eighteen. It is going to cost a lot, so I need to begin now.
Fifth, I am going to travel. I am not going to go abroad – not yet. But my family is going to visit Bukhara in spring, and I am going to take a lot of photographs.
Are these plans going to work? I don't know. Ask me again next December!
